a1-01.explain: Ask '¿Qué hora es?' (What time is it?). Answer with 'Son las + number' for two to twelve: Son las siete. One o'clock is singular: Es la una. Add 'de la mañana' (in the morning), 'de la tarde' (afternoon) or 'de la noche' (night). Watch out: never 'Son las una' or 'Es las dos'.
examples: Son las siete de la mañana.
It is seven in the morning.
Es la una de la tarde.
It is one in the afternoon.
—¿Qué hora es? —Son las ocho.
"What time is it?" "It's eight o'clock."

a1-01.explain: 'Hay' means both 'there is' and 'there are' and never changes: hay un olor, hay huevos. It says that something exists somewhere, usually with un/una, a number or no article. Watch out: to say where a specific, known thing is, use estar instead: Hay café en la mesa, but El café está en la mesa.
examples: En la casa de Lucía hay mucho ruido.
There is a lot of noise in Lucía's house.
Hay café, huevos, pan y leche.
There is coffee, eggs, bread and milk.
Hay leche en la mesa. La leche está en la mesa.
There is milk on the table. The milk is on the table.

a1-01.explain: 'Estar' says where someone is and how they feel right now: Papá está en la sala, Mamá está cansada. Forms: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están. Watch out: English uses one verb, 'to be', for everything, but Spanish uses estar (not ser) for location and for temporary states, so 'Mamá es cansada' is wrong here.
examples: Mamá está cansada.
Mom is tired.
Papá está en la sala.
Dad is in the living room.
Tomás está en la cocina.
Tomás is in the kitchen.

a1-01.explain: Present-tense endings change with the subject. Regular -ar verbs: preparo, preparas, prepara. Regular -er/-ir verbs: como, comes, come; vivo, vives, vive. 'Tener' (to have) is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene. Watch out: the Spanish present also covers English '-ing': 'Hoy yo preparo el desayuno' = Today I'm making breakfast.
examples: Lucía busca en el baño.
Lucía looks in the bathroom.
— ¡Hoy yo preparo el desayuno! —dice.
"Today I'm making breakfast!" he says.
Tiene el desayuno en la mesa.
He has breakfast on the table.

a1-02.explain: Use 'ser' for the day (Es sábado), for prices, and for what something is like (Es un desayuno rico). Ask prices with '¿Cuánto es?'. The verb agrees with the amount: Es un sol, but Son tres soles. Watch out: English says 'It's three soles', but Spanish says 'Son tres soles', never 'Es tres soles'.
examples: Es sábado y hay sol.
It is Saturday and it is sunny.
— ¿Cuánto es la naranja? —pregunta una señora.
"How much is the orange?" asks a lady.
— Son tres soles el kilo, señora.
"It's three soles a kilo, ma'am."

a1-02.explain: 'Gustar' works like 'to please': the thing you like is the subject. Use 'gusta' for one thing or an action and 'gustan' for plural things: me gusta la fruta, te gustan las uvas. 'Me' = to me, 'te' = to you. Watch out: don't say 'yo gusto' or 'te gusta las uvas'.
examples: — ¿Te gustan las uvas? —pregunta Mateo.
"Do you like grapes?" asks Mateo.
Me gusta la fruta.
I like fruit.
Me gustan las naranjas.
I like oranges.

a1-02.explain: 'Tener' (to have) is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen. To say you don't have something, put 'no' before the verb: no tengo dinero. Watch out: English adds 'don't' or uses 'no money'; Spanish simply puts 'no' before the verb and usually drops un/una: No tengo paraguas.
examples: Doña Elena tiene un puesto en el mercado.
Doña Elena has a stall at the market.
— Sí, pero no tengo dinero —dice el niño.
"Yes, but I have no money," says the boy.
¿Tienes una naranja?
Do you have an orange?

a1-02.explain: When a specific person receives the action (is seen, looked at, visited), Spanish puts 'a' before them. This 'a' is not translated. Things don't take it: Mateo mira a su abuela, but El niño mira las uvas. Watch out: a + el becomes al: Veo al niño.
examples: Mateo ve a un niño pequeño.
Mateo sees a small boy.
Mateo mira a su abuela.
Mateo looks at his grandmother.
El niño mira las uvas rojas.
The boy looks at the red grapes. (no 'a': grapes are things)

a1-03.topic: Telling time: son las / a las
a1-03.explain: '¿Qué hora es?' asks the time now; answer 'Son las ocho' (It's eight). '¿A qué hora…?' asks when something happens; answer 'A las doce' (At twelve). Watch out: English 'at' + time is 'a' in Spanish, so 'at one' is 'a la una', never 'en la una'.
examples: Hoy es lunes y son las ocho.
Today is Monday and it is eight o'clock.
A las doce, las niñas comen juntas.
At twelve, the girls eat together.
—¿A qué hora comen? —A la una.
"What time do they eat?" "At one."

a1-03.explain: Use 'ser' for what identifies someone: name, origin, nationality, job (es de Chile, es profesora). Use 'estar' for feelings and states right now (está nerviosa, está contenta). Watch out: English uses 'is' for both. 'Es nerviosa' would mean she is a nervous person by nature, not nervous today.
examples: Se llama Camila y es de Chile.
Her name is Camila and she is from Chile.
Está muy nerviosa.
She is very nervous.
La profesora es de México y hoy está contenta.
The teacher is from Mexico and today she is happy.

a1-03.topic: Gustar to say what you like
a1-03.explain: 'Me gusta' = I like, 'te gusta' = you like. Use 'gusta' with one thing or an infinitive (an action): me gusta el fútbol, me gusta dibujar. Use 'gustan' with plural things: me gustan los libros. To agree, say '¡A mí también!' (Me too!). Watch out: never 'me gusto' or 'me gustan dibujar'.
examples: — Camila, ¿te gusta el fútbol? —pregunta.
"Camila, do you like soccer?" she asks.
— No, me gusta dibujar —responde Camila.
"No, I like to draw," answers Camila.
— ¡A mí también! —dice Ana.
"Me too!" says Ana.

a1-03.explain: 'Tener' means 'to have' (tengo, tienes, tiene). Spanish also uses it where English uses 'to be' for some feelings: tener hambre (to be hungry), tener sed (to be thirsty), tener frío (to be cold). Watch out: say 'Tengo hambre', not 'Estoy hambre'. 'Hambre' is a noun, so 'very hungry' is 'mucha hambre'.
examples: Tiene el pelo largo y negro.
She has long black hair.
Ana tiene un bocadillo de queso.
Ana has a cheese sandwich.
— ¿Tienes hambre? —pregunta Ana.
"Are you hungry?" asks Ana.

a1-04.explain: 'Querer' (to want) and 'poder' (can, to be able to) are followed directly by an infinitive: quiere ir, puedes tomar. Both change their stem: quiero, quieres, quiere; puedo, puedes, puede. Querer can also take a noun: quiero mi paraguas. Watch out: no extra word for 'to': 'quiere ir', not 'quiere a ir'.
examples: Julia quiere ir a la escuela.
Julia wants to go to school.
— No, pero puedes tomar este azul —dice el tío.
"No, but you can take this blue one," says her uncle.
— Quiero mi paraguas rojo porque es mi favorito.
"I want my red umbrella because it is my favorite."

a1-04.explain: 'Ir' (to go) is irregular: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. Put 'a' (to) before the place: va a la tienda. Watch out: a + el contracts to 'al' (va al mercado, never 'a el'), and 'home' is just 'a casa', with no article. 'Va' can mean 'goes' or 'is going'.
examples: Julia va a la tienda de su tío.
Julia goes to her uncle's shop.
Julia va al mercado con su papá.
Julia goes to the market with her dad.
Las dos van a casa muy contentas.
The two of them go home very happy.

a1-04.explain: To make a sentence negative, put 'no' right before the verb: no está, no tengo. If there is a small pronoun such as 'lo' (it), 'no' goes before the pronoun: Yo no lo tengo. Watch out: Spanish has no helper verb like 'don't/doesn't', so 'I don't have' is simply 'no tengo'.
examples: No está en la sala.
It is not in the living room.
Papá dice: — Yo no lo tengo, Julia.
Dad says, "I don't have it, Julia."
Su amiga Sara no tiene paraguas.
Her friend Sara has no umbrella.

a1-04.explain: '¿Dónde está…?' asks where one specific thing or person is ('¿Dónde están…?' for plural). It uses estar, never ser or hay. 'Porque' (one word, no accent) means 'because' and gives a reason; the question 'why?' is '¿Por qué?' (two words, accent). '¡Allí está!' = There it is!
examples: — ¿Dónde está mi paraguas rojo? —pregunta.
"Where is my red umbrella?" she asks.
¡Allí está el paraguas rojo!
There is the red umbrella!
— Quiero mi paraguas rojo porque es mi favorito.
"I want my red umbrella because it is my favorite."

a1-05.explain: 'Hay' = there is / there are; 'no hay' = there isn't / there aren't. It never changes for plural. Watch out: 'no' goes before hay ('no hay', never 'hay no'), and after 'no hay' Spanish usually drops the article: no hay huevos = there are no eggs / there aren't any eggs.
examples: En la cocina hay leche y azúcar.
In the kitchen there is milk and sugar.
Pero no hay huevos.
But there are no eggs.
—¿Hay azúcar? —Sí, hay.
"Is there any sugar?" "Yes, there is."

a1-05.explain: 'Querer' (to want), 'necesitar' (to need) and 'poder' (can) are followed by an infinitive: quieren hacer, no puedo comprar. Only the first verb changes for the subject; the second stays in the infinitive. Querer and necesitar can also take a noun: necesitamos huevos. Watch out: querer and poder change their stem (quieren, puedo); necesitar is regular.
examples: Sofía y Diego quieren hacer un pastel.
Sofía and Diego want to make a cake.
— Necesitamos huevos, leche y azúcar —dice Sofía.
"We need eggs, milk and sugar," says Sofía.
— No puedo comprar los huevos —dice triste.
"I can't buy the eggs," he says sadly.

a1-05.explain: 'Voy' is the 'I' form of ir (to go): 'Voy a la tienda' = I'm going to the store. 'A' means 'to' before a place, and a + el = al (voy al mercado). Watch out: 'voy a + place' says where you go, but 'voy a + infinitive' says what you're going to do: voy a comprar huevos.
examples: — Voy a la tienda —dice Diego.
"I'm going to the store," says Diego.
Voy al mercado con mi abuela.
I'm going to the market with my grandma.
Voy a comprar huevos.
I'm going to buy eggs.

a1-05.explain: Use 'a las + number' to say at what time something happens: a las seis = at six. For one o'clock, say 'a la una'. Ask with '¿A qué hora…?' (At what time…?). Watch out: 'Son las seis' means 'It is six'; 'A las seis' means 'At six'. Spanish never uses 'en' with clock times.
examples: A las seis, la abuela abre la puerta.
At six, Grandma opens the door.
—¿A qué hora es la fiesta? —A las seis.
"What time is the party?" "At six."
La abuela come a la una.
Grandma eats at one.

a1-06.explain: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun that matches the subject: me levanto (I get up), te levantas (you get up), se levanta (he/she gets up). The pronoun is a separate word before the conjugated verb. Many daily-routine verbs work this way: levantarse, ducharse, sentarse, llamarse. Watch out: English often has no 'myself' here, but Spanish needs the pronoun.
examples: Todos los días me levanto a las seis.
Every day I get up at six.
Me ducho y tomo un café con leche.
I take a shower and have a coffee with milk.
Un señor mayor se sienta a mi lado.
An older man sits down next to me.

a1-06.explain: For 'I', regular present verbs end in -o: trabajar → trabajo, responder → respondo, vivir → vivo. Because the -o already shows 'I', Spanish usually leaves out 'yo' (use it for emphasis or contrast). Watch out: some very common verbs are irregular in the yo form: soy, estoy, voy, tengo.
examples: Me llamo Lucía y vivo en Valencia.
My name is Lucía and I live in Valencia.
Me ducho y tomo un café con leche.
I take a shower and have a coffee with milk.
—No, trabajo en una librería —respondo yo.
"No, I work in a bookstore," I answer.

a1-06.explain: Use 'estar' to say where a person or thing is: La parada está cerca de mi calle. Useful partners: cerca de (near), lejos de (far from), al lado de (next to), en (in/on). Watch out: for where a known thing is, the standard verb is estar, not ser or hay: 'Mi trabajo está lejos'. And de + el = del.
examples: Mi trabajo está muy lejos de mi casa.
My job is very far from my house.
La parada está cerca de mi calle.
The stop is near my street.
El hospital está al lado del parque.
The hospital is next to the park.

a1-06.explain: 'Me gusta' = I like (literally 'it pleases me'). Use 'gusta' with one thing or an infinitive and 'gustan' with plural things. 'Mucho' (a lot) goes after the verb: me gusta mucho. Watch out: 'I like it' is just 'me gusta', with no word for 'it', and 'I don't like' is 'no me gusta'.
examples: Me gusta mucho mi viaje en autobús.
I like my bus ride very much.
Me gusta leer en el autobús.
I like to read on the bus.
No me gustan los lunes.
I don't like Mondays.

a1-07.explain: 'Estar' tells where someone is and how they are now: está en un café, está mojada. Use 'está' for one person or thing and 'están' for more than one: ellos están contentos. Watch out: 'la ropa' (clothes) is singular in Spanish, so it's 'su ropa está mojada', even though English says 'her clothes are'.
examples: Ana está en un café pequeño.
Ana is in a small café.
No tiene paraguas y su ropa está mojada.
She has no umbrella and her clothes are wet.
Ana y Tomás están contentos.
Ana and Tomás are happy.

a1-07.explain: 'Hay' (there is / there are) introduces something that exists in a place, often for the first time: hay una mesa libre. It never changes for plural: hay dos mesas. Watch out: use hay with un/una, numbers or no article; to talk about a specific thing (esta silla, la mesa), use estar: ¿Está libre esta silla?
examples: Hay una mesa libre cerca de la ventana.
There is a free table near the window.
—Sí, claro, hay mucho espacio —dice Ana.
"Yes, of course, there is a lot of room," says Ana.
—Perdón, ¿está libre esta silla?
"Excuse me, is this chair free?"

a1-07.explain: 'Se' before a verb marks a reflexive verb in the he/she form: se sienta (sits down, literally 'seats herself'), se llama (is called, literally 'calls himself'). With 'I' it is 'me': me siento, me llamo. Watch out: 'Ana sienta' without 'se' is wrong, and sentarse changes e → ie: me siento, se sienta.
examples: Ana se sienta y pide un chocolate caliente.
Ana sits down and orders a hot chocolate.
Se llama Tomás y también está mojado.
His name is Tomás and he is wet too.
Me llamo Ana.
My name is Ana.

a1-07.topic: Present tense with vivir and leer
a1-07.explain: Regular -er and -ir verbs share these endings: -o (yo), -es (tú), -e (él/ella): leo, lees, lee; vivo, vives, vive. Watch out: the simple present also covers English 'I am reading': 'Yo también leo ese libro' = I'm reading that book too. You don't need a separate -ing form.
examples: Al final, Tomás pregunta: —¿Dónde vives?
In the end, Tomás asks, "Where do you live?"
—Vivo en la calle Veinte, cerca del parque —responde Ana.
"I live on Twenty Street, near the park," answers Ana.
—Yo también leo ese libro —dice Ana.
"I am reading that book too," says Ana.

a1-08.explain: 'Tener que' + infinitive means 'have to' or 'must': tienes que regar (you have to water). Only tener changes: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que. Watch out: don't drop 'que' ('tengo venir' is wrong), and don't confuse it with 'tengo' alone, which just means 'I have'.
examples: —Tienes que regar las plantas conmigo, y las flores son tuyas.
"You have to water the plants with me, and the flowers are yours."
—De nada. Tienes que venir otra vez mañana —sonríe ella.
"You're welcome. You have to come again tomorrow," she smiles.
Tengo que ir al mercado.
I have to go to the market.

a1-08.explain: To compare, use 'más + adjective + que' = 'more … than' or '-er than': más grande que (bigger than), más bonitas que (prettier than). The adjective still agrees with the noun: las flores son más bonitas. Watch out: use 'que', not 'de' or 'como'. For 'better', say 'mejor'.
examples: El jardín es más grande que su casa.
The garden is bigger than her house.
—Mis flores son más bonitas que las del mercado —dice ella.
"My flowers are prettier than the ones at the market," she says.
Mi casa es más pequeña que tu casa.
My house is smaller than your house.

a1-08.explain: Spanish uses 'tener' for age: Nico tiene diez años = Nico is ten (literally 'has ten years'). Ask: ¿Cuántos años tienes? (How old are you?). Tener also means to have or own: tiene un jardín. Watch out: never use ser or estar for age ('Nico es diez años' is wrong), and don't leave out 'años'.
examples: Nico tiene diez años y vive en Oaxaca.
Nico is ten years old and lives in Oaxaca.
—¿Cuántos años tienes? —Tengo diez años.
"How old are you?" "I'm ten."
Su vecina, la señora Elena, tiene un jardín.
His neighbor, Mrs. Elena, has a garden.

a1-08.explain: '¿Por qué?' (two words, with an accent) asks 'why?'. 'Porque' (one word, no accent) answers 'because'. Watch out: they sound almost the same, so the difference shows in writing: question = ¿por qué?, answer = porque.
examples: —Nico, ¿por qué estás triste? —pregunta ella.
"Nico, why are you sad?" she asks.
Está triste porque solo tiene veinte pesos.
He is sad because he only has twenty pesos.
—¿Por qué? —Porque no tengo dinero.
"Why?" "Because I don't have any money."

a1-09.topic: Ir a + infinitive: the near future
a1-09.explain: 'Ir a' + infinitive talks about the future, like English 'going to': voy a cocinar, vas a hacer, va a estar. Pattern: voy/vas/va/vamos/van + a + infinitive. Watch out: don't drop the 'a' ('vas hacer' is wrong), and don't conjugate the second verb ('vas a haces' is wrong).
examples: —El sábado es mi cumpleaños y voy a estar sola.
"Saturday is my birthday and I'm going to be alone."
—Entonces, ¿qué vas a hacer el sábado?
"So, what are you going to do on Saturday?"
—Voy a cocinar una tortilla y ver una película.
"I'm going to cook a tortilla and watch a movie."

a1-09.explain: Question words carry a written accent: ¿qué? (what), ¿por qué? (why), ¿dónde? (where), ¿cómo? (how), ¿cuándo? (when), ¿quién? (who). Written questions open with ¿ and close with ?. '¿Qué tal estás?' = How are you? Watch out: '¿Qué dices?' literally asks 'What are you saying?', but often shows surprise, like 'What?!'
examples: —¡Hola, Marta! ¿Qué tal estás?
"Hi, Marta! How are you?"
—¿Por qué estás triste? —pregunta él.
"Why are you sad?" he asks.
—¿Qué dices? ¡Tú vives en Madrid!
"What are you saying? You live in Madrid!"

a1-09.topic: Ser for time, estar for feelings
a1-09.explain: Use 'ser' for the day and the time: Es viernes, Son las dos. Use 'estar' for how you feel and where you are: Estoy bien, Estoy en Sevilla. 'Estoy' is the 'I' form of estar. Watch out: 'I'm fine' is always 'Estoy bien'; 'Soy bien' is wrong.
examples: Es viernes por la tarde y suena el teléfono.
It is Friday afternoon and the phone rings.
—Hola, Javier. Estoy bien, pero un poco triste.
"Hi, Javier. I'm fine, but a little sad."
—Sí, pero ahora estoy en Sevilla, delante de tu edificio.
"Yes, but right now I'm in Seville, in front of your building."

a1-09.explain: With days of the week, Spanish uses 'el' where English uses 'on': el sábado = on Saturday. 'Los sábados' = on Saturdays (every week). Days are written in lowercase. Watch out: don't add 'en': 'en el sábado' is wrong.
examples: —Entonces, ¿qué vas a hacer el sábado?
"So, what are you going to do on Saturday?"
El sábado no va a estar sola.
On Saturday she is not going to be alone.
Los sábados como con mi familia.
On Saturdays I eat with my family.

a1-10.explain: 'Ir a' + infinitive says what people are going to do: voy a, vas a, va a, vamos a, van a + infinitive. 'Vamos a ir a la playa' has two a's: one for the future, one meaning 'to' the beach. Watch out: 'vamos a + infinitive' can also mean 'let's…': ¡Vamos a comer! = Let's eat!
examples: —El sábado vamos a ir a la playa —dice Elena.
"On Saturday we are going to go to the beach," says Elena.
—Entonces el abuelo va a venir con nosotros.
"Then Grandpa is going to come with us."
Los tres van a pasar un día perfecto.
The three of them are going to have a perfect day.

a1-10.explain: 'El sábado' = on Saturday; 'a las ocho' = at eight. With a clock time, use 'de la mañana / de la tarde / de la noche': a las ocho de la mañana. Without a clock time, use 'por la mañana / por la tarde / por la noche': el viernes por la noche. Watch out: no 'en' before days.
examples: —A Cádiz. El tren sale a las ocho de la mañana.
"To Cádiz. The train leaves at eight in the morning."
El viernes por la noche, los hermanos preparan las mochilas.
On Friday night, the siblings pack their backpacks.
El sábado, los tres llegan a la estación temprano.
On Saturday, the three of them arrive at the station early.

a1-10.explain: 'Estar' tells where people or things are: están en la cocina, ¿Dónde están…?, Aquí están. Use 'está' for one and 'están' for more than one. Watch out: 'Aquí están' = Here they are; Spanish needs no word for 'they' because the verb ending shows it. Don't use 'son' or 'hay' for where known things are.
examples: Elena y su hermano Raúl están en la cocina.
Elena and her brother Raúl are in the kitchen.
—¿Dónde están los billetes? —grita él.
"Where are the tickets?" he shouts.
—Aquí están. Yo los tengo.
"Here they are. I have them."

a1-10.explain: To compare, use 'más + adjective + que': más grande que = bigger than. For age, Spanish uses 'tener', not 'ser': Él tiene ochenta años = He is eighty years old (literally 'has eighty years'). Watch out: 'más grande de' and 'es ochenta años' are typical English-speaker mistakes.
examples: —Es más grande que en mis recuerdos —dice.
"It is bigger than in my memories," he says.
—Perfecto. Él tiene ochenta años y quiere ver el mar.
"Perfect. He is eighty years old and wants to see the sea."
El mar es más grande que el lago.
The sea is bigger than the lake.
